title: Canada PGWP Refusal Rate Hits 25% as Portal Flaws Trip Up Indian Graduates
excerpt: A flawed IRCC application portal has driven a surge in Post-Graduation Work Permit rejections, with immigration lawyers urging affected Indian graduates to seek reconsideration or judicial review before strict deadlines expire.
body:
• Canada's PGWP refusal rate climbed past 25% by late 2025, up sharply from prior years, with most rejections linked to missing language test documents.
  • IRCC's application portal lacks a dedicated upload field for mandatory language results introduced in November 2024, causing graduates to omit documents they actually possessed.
  • Affected graduates have three options — reconsideration via IRCC webform, judicial review within 15 days, or a new application — but strict deadlines make immediate legal advice critical.
  • Indian students face compounded risk as Canada's TRIS fraud-screening framework routes applications from high-risk countries through heightened scrutiny, including PGWP applications from former SDS permit holders.

Canada's Post-Graduation Work Permit refusal rate has climbed past 25%, according to immigration analysts and internal projections, turning what was once a routine pathway to Canadian work experience into a minefield for international graduates — a disproportionate number of them Indian.

The surge in rejections is not driven by ineligible applicants. Immigration lawyers across Canada say most refusals stem from a single systemic failure: the Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) online application portal does not include a dedicated upload field for language test results, a document that became mandatory for all PGWP applicants on November 1, 2024.

"Refusals are being issued through an automated system, resulting in applicants being refused en masse for failing to upload a document they were never prompted to upload during the application process."

— Will Tao, Vancouver immigration lawyer, quoted in the Toronto Star

A Portal Problem, Not an Eligibility Problem

Under rules introduced in late 2024, all PGWP applicants must submit proof of English or French language proficiency — CLB 7 for university degree holders, CLB 5 for college diploma and certificate graduates. Accepted tests include IELTS General Training, CELPIP-General, TEF Canada, TCF Canada, and PTE Core, with results valid for two years.

https://x.com/MannyLidher/status/2079992823722709423

But IRCC's portal provides no designated upload slot for these results. Applicants must instead upload them under a generic "Client Information" section — a workaround buried in a separate policy document on IRCC's website, not visible within the application portal itself. Many graduates had completed the required tests and met the benchmarks but never uploaded the results because the portal gave them no indication they were needed, according to immigration law firm Green and Spiegel.

Between November 1, 2024, and December 31, 2025, IRCC received more than 302,000 PGWP applications. Of those, 945 were rejected specifically for language-related reasons, according to a spokesperson for Immigration Minister Lena Diab's office quoted by CIC News. Immigration lawyers say the true number of affected graduates is likely higher, as many refusals cite missing documents without specifying the language test.

IRCC acknowledged the system issue in December 2025 and updated its Program Delivery Instructions to clarify where results should be uploaded. A spokesperson confirmed that a dedicated upload field is now under development as part of broader IT improvements, though no implementation date has been announced, according to CIC News.

Options for Refused Applicants — and Tight Deadlines

Immigration lawyers are urging affected graduates to act immediately. The PGWP is non-renewable, non-replaceable, and available only once — making a refusal potentially career-ending for graduates who planned to use Canadian work experience as a pathway to permanent residency.

Green and Spiegel, one of Canada's oldest immigration law firms, outlined three options for refused applicants. First, a reconsideration request can be submitted through IRCC's webform, ideally within 30 days of the refusal. Some applicants have received positive outcomes, with IRCC reopening applications after receiving supporting documentation.

Second, applicants can file for judicial review in Federal Court — but the deadline is just 15 days from the date of refusal for in-Canada applicants. "In many cases, our office pursues early settlement discussions with Department of Justice counsel representing IRCC to facilitate the reopening of the application without the need to proceed through the full judicial review process," the firm stated.

Third, graduates still within the 180-day window from their completion date may submit a new PGWP application, though IRCC's processing delays mean many refusals arrive after this window has closed. Restoration of status must be requested within 90 days of losing status.

Compounded Risk for Indian Graduates

Indian students face additional scrutiny under Canada's Temporary Resident Integrity Strategy (TRIS), a fraud-screening framework that routes applications from high-risk countries through heightened review. A March 2026 Auditor General report confirmed India is designated as a high-risk country, with study permit approval rates for Indian applicants dropping from 77% in 2023 to below 25% in 2025.

The Auditor General's report also recommended that IRCC strengthen controls for study permit extensions by reviewing applicants originally approved under the now-closed Student Direct Stream (SDS), which had a 98% approval rate despite India's high-risk designation. This means Indian students who entered Canada on SDS permits now face additional scrutiny when applying for PGWPs — the SDS approval itself has become a risk signal.

Canada approved just 75,372 new study permits in all of 2025, a 64% drop year-on-year and below COVID-era levels, according to Collegedunia analysis of IRCC data. For Indian graduates already in Canada who completed their studies and met every eligibility requirement, a PGWP refusal due to a portal design flaw adds insult to an already hostile immigration environment.

What's Next

IRCC's promised portal fix remains undated. In the interim, immigration lawyers and regulated consultants recommend that applicants combine all mandatory documents — language test results, field-of-study proof, and a cover letter — into a single PDF labeled "Letter of Explanation, Mandatory Documents" and upload it under the optional documents section.

For graduates whose applications have already been refused, the window for action is narrow. McInnes Cooper, an Atlantic Canadian law firm that has seen a rise in PGWP refusal cases, advised that applicants whose study permits are still valid can submit a new work permit application, while those with expired permits must first apply for restoration of student status before reapplying — all within the 180-day completion window.

With an estimated 1.1 million international students in Canada — Indians comprising the largest single cohort — the PGWP remains the most direct pathway to Canadian work experience and permanent residency. Immigration advocates say the current refusal crisis demands not just a portal fix, but a systemic rethink of how IRCC communicates rule changes to applicants already in the pipeline.
